findings.headline: No households were placed in bed and breakfast accommodation during Q2, with 16 households in emergency accommodation
findings.detail: The paper states that the number of households in emergency accommodation fell compared with previous quarters, which it attributes mainly to more temporary accommodation available from registered providers. It also reports that average weeks in emergency accommodation or B&B rose to 4 because of two complex cases where move-on was not possible.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation placements are a recognised cost pressure for councils, so a quarter with no B&B placements and a lower emergency accommodation count is a figure a finance director would compare with their own temporary accommodation budget.
findings.figures: 0 households placed in B&B in Q2; 16 households in emergency accommodation; average 4 weeks in emergency accommodation or B&B
findings.quote: No households were placed in Bed and Breakfast accommodation during Q2.

findings.headline: Affordable homes delivered reached 45 year to date at Q2, against 75 expected at the half-year point, with forecast completions of 152 against an annual target above 150
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Q2 shortfall to delays on the Land East of Horndean development with legal agreements, and notes that homes are delivered according to contractor programmes. It also flags further risk from the Registered Providers sector on s106 housing.
findings.matters: Section 106 affordable housing completions that are 30 homes behind a straight-line profile, with little margin in the forecast, affect the s106 income and housing-delivery commitments that other councils also depend on.
findings.figures: 45 homes year to date; 75 expected at half-year; 30 behind straight-line profile; forecast completions 152; annual target above 150 homes
findings.quote: Risks exist to achieving the target as forecast completions are 152, leaving little margin.

findings.headline: The Leader wrote to MHCLG on 11 September 2026 requesting reclamation of costs incurred on Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The paper records that the Government withdrew the decision to implement option 1a for Hampshire on 07 September 2026 and paused the LGR programme. A Government review was commissioned, with an update expected by the end of October 2026.
findings.matters: A council asking central government to reimburse reorganisation costs after a withdrawn decision is a live question for any council in a reorganisation process, and it bears directly on how those costs are recorded and recovered.
findings.quote: The Leader sent a letter to MHCLG on 11 September 2026 requesting reclamation of costs incurred.

findings.headline: External grant and inward investment funding for growth or placemaking projects was £0 at Q2, against £29,500 expected at the half-year point
findings.detail: The paper says future opportunities are expected to be primarily routed through devolution arrangements and the HSCCA, which are still evolving. It says limited opportunities from other sources are being sought for Whitehill and Bordon, and it expects bidding activity to increase in Q3-4.
findings.matters: A council that has secured no external funding at mid-year against a half-year expectation of £29,500 is relying on bids and devolution timing, which other councils planning similar growth funding will want to compare.
findings.figures: £0 secured at Q2 (expected £29,500 at the half-year point); year-end cumulative target £59,000
findings.quote: secured (expected: £29,500 at the half-year point).

findings.headline: Value of financial business support given reached £209,000 by Q2, against £100,000 expected at the half-year point
findings.detail: The paper says the council has two main grant programmes for businesses. A £200k reserve funding grant programme has assisted 8 rural enterprises, and an extra £9k was provided for a business mentoring scheme in Whitehill and Bordon.
findings.matters: The paper shows a reserve being drawn down to fund a business grant programme, and the year-to-date value has already passed the annual target, which a finance officer will want to see against the reserve's remaining balance.
findings.figures: £209,000 year to date (expected £100,000 at half-year); annual target exceeded by £9,000; £200k reserve funding; 8 rural enterprises assisted
findings.quote: Annual target already exceeded by £9,000.

findings.headline: CIL and S106 monitoring fees collected in Q2 were £71,616.27, and the paper says CIL and Section 106 income has exceeded the annual target by mid-year
findings.detail: The paper says the income offsets the cost of the developer contributions service and depends on when development commences. It notes that commencements have been high this year, but says it is impossible to know whether this will continue.
findings.matters: Developer contribution income that has passed its annual budget at mid-year is unusual, and the paper's own caveat that it is hard to predict is the point a finance officer elsewhere would want to check against their own forecast.
findings.figures: £71,616.27 collected in Q2; annual target £72,300 (year-end cumulative); £36,150 needed at the half-year point
findings.quote: CIL and Section 106 income has exceeded the annual target by the midpoint of the year.

findings.headline: Council Tax cash collection stood at 57.45% cumulative at Q2 against a year-end target above 98.3%, and business rates at 57.69% against above 97.9%
findings.detail: The paper says Council Tax collection is slightly below the equivalent point in 2025/26, with recovery action and direct debit promotion continuing. For business rates it says performance is slightly ahead of the equivalent point in 2025/26, and both indicators are described as stable.
findings.matters: Mid-year collection rates are the first read on whether the council will meet its tax-base income assumptions, and the year-end target gap is what a finance director will need to track through Q3.
findings.figures: Council Tax 57.45% cumulative (Q1 26/27 29.32%), target above 98.3%; Business rates 57.69% cumulative (Q1 26/27 30.31%), target above 97.9%
findings.quote: Council Tax collection performance at QRC2 is slightly below the equivalent position in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Finance Directorate reported a £0.183m adverse Q2 budget variance, while Operations reported £0.275m favourable and Corporate Services £0.074m favourable
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Finance adverse variance to increased insurance, banking and audit costs, and the Operations favourable variance mainly to vacancies, higher planning income and a one-off housing strategy fee. The Modern and Efficient Council section separately states that directorate budget variance data was unavailable for reporting.
findings.matters: The paper shows a directorate overspend driven by insurance, banking and audit costs, and it offsets that against vacancy savings, which is a pattern other finance officers will recognise.
findings.figures: Finance £0.183m adverse (Q1 26/27 £0.096m); Operations £0.275m favourable; Corporate Services £0.074m favourable
findings.quote: This adverse variance has been caused by increase in insurance, banking, and audit costs.

findings.headline: Sundry debt outstanding rose to £891,768 at Q2 from £808,667 at Q1, an increase of £83,101 (+10.3%)
findings.detail: The paper attributes the rise under 30 days to quarterly investment property rents raised but not yet paid, and the rise in 31-60 days mainly to one £20,195 invoice being chased. Debt over 365 days fell slightly to £440,024, and the paper describes long-standing debt as remaining high.
findings.matters: Rising sundry debt, and a long-standing balance that the council says it is still recovering, bear on the cash position and bad-debt provision of a council that depends on rental and other sundry income.
findings.figures: £891,768 total outstanding at Q2 26/27; £808,667 at Q1 26/27; increase of £83,101 (+10.3%); over 365 days £440,024; 31-60 days increase of £37,427 (+191.8%)
findings.quote: Sundry debt increased during the quarter and long-standing debt remains high.

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY reports response times to its sample queries as "long overdue" in areas including PPE, cash flow statement, leases, creditors, provisions and income.
findings.detail: EY says management needs to focus on responding to these queries so that EY can complete work in those areas. The list also includes Revenue Expenditure Funded from Capital Under Statute additions and high-level queries on the draft statement of accounts submitted at the end of June 2026.
findings.matters: Slow responses to audit queries delay the timetable for the whole audit, and finance teams at other councils face the same pressure when their finance staff are stretched by closing accounts.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The are a number of areas where the response time to our existing sample queries is long overdue, particularly Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE), cash flow statement, leases, creditors, provisions, income

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY says it is hopeful that at least some of the October 2026 amendments can be audited by the 31 January 2027 backstop date, and that the audit may run beyond December 2026.
findings.detail: The timetable is subject to audit resources and the council's finance team's capacity, and EY's Audit Committee update in December depends on whether the initial procedures are complete. The audit certificate also depends on Whole of Government Accounts work, for which NAO instructions have not yet been issued.
findings.matters: A council that misses the 31 January backstop date for its accounts can face a modified or disclaimed opinion, which affects how peers and lenders read its position.
findings.figures: Backstop date 31 January 2027
findings.quote: we are hopeful that the audit of at least some of these areas can be achieved by the backstop date of 31 January 2027.

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: Management has made a series of adjustments in October 2026 to the published statement of accounts, affecting PPE, reserves and capital grants received in advance.
findings.detail: EY says these errors were brought to its attention during October, and some relate to areas subject to the disclaimed opinion in 2024/25. EY has not yet reviewed them in detail, may not do so by the December committee meeting, and plans to address them after its initial procedures.
findings.matters: Post-publication restatements to PPE and reserves, after a disclaimed opinion in the prior year, are the kind of late correction other councils and lenders would want to know about.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Management have made a series of adjustments to the published statement of accounts impacting PPE (Other land and buildings, infrastructure assets, right of use assets),

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY reports that the 2025/26 draft statement of accounts was prepared on the IFRS 16 leases basis, after the 2024/25 accounts were not and received a modified opinion.
findings.detail: EY says testing of a sample of leases is in progress, and no significant issues have been identified so far from testing the process and individual lease assessments. It has one outstanding question because not all items from the prior period adjustment appear to have been posted to the ledger.
findings.matters: Moving to the IFRS 16 basis for the first time caused a modified opinion for the council in 2024/25, and peers adopting the same standard face the same transition issues.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: However, the 2025/26 draft statement of accounts submitted at the end of June 2026 was prepared on the correct basis.

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY reports fewer formatting, casting and internal consistency errors in the June 2026 draft statement of accounts, and the draft includes the IFRS 16 disclosures and cash flow statement missing from the 2024/25 draft.
findings.detail: EY says the quality improvement is still being assessed, and it will decide once all procedures are complete whether a significant weakness in the council's arrangements still exists under the prior-year value-for-money criteria on budgetary control and financial reporting. That 2024/25 weakness was reported by exception.
findings.matters: A value-for-money significant weakness on financial reporting, reported by exception, is a public marker of governance, and the draft's quality is what EY will use to decide whether it remains.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: we have noted fewer formatting, casting and internal consistency errors, and the statement of accounts included the required IFRS 16 disclosures and a cash flow statement which were not present in the initial draft submitted for audit in 204/25.

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY has identified audit differences including a £297k judgemental overstatement of the NNDR appeals provision and a £5m misclassification between short-term investments and cash.
findings.detail: EY lists three audit differences: the £5m misclassification between short-term investments and cash and cash equivalents, the £297k overstatement of the NNDR appeals provision, and a £444k misclassification between General Fund debtors and Housing Benefit overpayments. EY says it has found fewer errors and less need for extended testing than in the previous two years.
findings.matters: The appeals provision is a judgement area that depends on assumptions about business rates appeals, which finance directors at other billing authorities also have to estimate.
findings.figures: £5m misclassification; £297k NNDR appeals provision overstatement; £444k debtors and Housing Benefit overpayments misclassification; £1.075m overall materiality
findings.quote: Judgmental overstatement of £297k in relation to the NNDR appeals provision

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY has gained assurance over £18.7m of the £22.878m sampled from capital grant balances that stood at £24.6m at 31 March 2025.
findings.detail: The balances relate to Capital Grants Received in Advance and Capital Grants Unapplied, and a prior period adjustment is in dispute. Management now suggests a further prior period adjustment reducing the 2024/25 published values, and EY has not yet been given the journals for the earlier correction.
findings.matters: Capital grant balances that are being restated across two years, with journals still outstanding, affect how reserves and capital financing are presented, which other councils with similar grant balances will recognise.
findings.figures: £24.6 million balance at 31 March 2025; £22.878 million sampled; £18.7 million assured
findings.quote: We have sampled a total of £22.878 million and have been able to gain assurances over the valuation of £18.7 million.

findings.paper_title: 1.1 26 EHDC - Progress Report to TCWG - November 2026
findings.headline: EY reports an unreconciled £7.7m difference between the financial statements and the council tax and business rate accounting models, with the council's external specialist work not expected to finish before the backstop date.
findings.detail: Management has engaged an external specialist to resolve the difference, but EY says the work is not expected to be completed before the backstop date. EY states that if the balances are not reconciled, another modified opinion will follow, after modified opinions for 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.matters: A modified opinion on the accounts of a council with a material unreconciled difference in its council tax and business rates balances is the kind of audit outcome that finance directors and lenders track across councils.
findings.figures: £7.7m unreconciled difference
findings.quote: Management have engaged an external specialist to resolve an unreconciled difference of £7.7m between the financial statements and the council tax and business rate accounting models.

findings.paper_title: 2.2 EHDC Audit Committee Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Appendix 1)_1
findings.headline: Southern Internal Audit Partnership reports 30% of the 2026-27 audit plan completed against a 90% target.
findings.detail: The performance measures also show 33% of audits delivered to draft report within agreed timescales against an 80% target, and 0% delivered to final report within timescales against an 80% target. The paper does not give a reason for the shortfall.
findings.matters: A slow delivery of the audit plan affects when the assurance behind the annual governance statement arrives, which is relevant to any finance director relying on that timetable.
findings.figures: 30% of plan completed (target 90%); 33% to draft within timescales (target 80%); 0% to final within timescales (target 80%)
findings.quote: Percentage of the agreed audit plan completed (issue of draft / final report) Ongoing 90% 30%

findings.paper_title: 2.2 EHDC Audit Committee Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Appendix 1)_1
findings.headline: Management has confirmed all actions closed in eight earlier review areas since the August 2026 report, including Risk Management and Asset Management – Investment Properties.
findings.detail: The eight closed review areas include Risk Management (June 2026), which had received a Limited opinion, and Asset Management – Investment Properties (June 2026), which had received a Substantial opinion. Core Finance Systems – Follow-up (July 2026) is also on the list.
findings.matters: Closure of the Risk Management actions after a Limited opinion is a point of comparison for finance directors whose own risk management audits have been limited.
findings.figures: eight review areas closed; Risk Management opinion Limited (final report 22.06.26); Asset Management – Investment Properties opinion Substantial (final report 19.06.26)
findings.quote: all actions have been completed / closed in respect of eight previous review areas

findings.paper_title: 2.2 EHDC Audit Committee Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Appendix 1)_1
findings.headline: Parking & Enforcement has agreed to write back older debt on a backlog of over 500 cases, with the full review due by 30.11.26.
findings.detail: The audit found PCNs were being issued well, but a backlog of over 500 cases had no debt recovery action, dating back at least six years. The service's latest update, dated 15.10.26, records the decision to write back older debt and target future debt. The revised due date for the high-priority action is 30.11.26.
findings.matters: A decision to write back older parking debt reduces the income that was carried in the accounts, and other councils with similar PCN backlogs would be interested in how the write-back was handled.
findings.figures: over 500 cases; over 200 arising since March 2024; revised due date 30.11.26
findings.quote: Agreed to write back older debt and target future debt.

findings.paper_title: 2.2 EHDC Audit Committee Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Appendix 1)_1
findings.headline: Procurement audit found two suppliers with 2025-26 purchase orders over £10K not on the Contracts Register, one paid over £300K.
findings.detail: One supplier was paid over £300K under a collaborative procurement led by another authority, but the Cabinet report on that spend did not say which authority selected the supplier. The second supplier had no payments at the time of testing, and its commitment was not linked to a contract or a collaborative procurement. The audit also found no Finance or Procurement analysis to detect off-contract spend.
findings.matters: Spend with suppliers outside the contracts register is a control gap that other councils running collaborative procurements would want to check against their own registers.
findings.figures: purchase orders over £10K; one supplier paid over £300K
findings.quote: Two of the suppliers were not present on the Contracts Register.

findings.paper_title: 2.2 EHDC Audit Committee Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Appendix 1)_1
findings.headline: Procurement audit, finalised 06.10.26, gave Limited assurance with 2 High, 2 Medium and 1 Low management actions.
findings.detail: The audit found good practice against Contract Standing Orders and the Procurement Act 2023, but also found no procurement strategy and no procurement KPIs reported to senior managers or Members. One high-priority action is still pending, with the paper saying it is intended to be in place by the end of March 2027, when contract data moves into Unit 4.
findings.matters: A finance director at any council can compare the Limited opinion, the missing procurement strategy and the Unit 4 migration timetable against their own procurement controls.
findings.figures: 2 High 2 Medium 1 Low management actions; high-priority action intended in place by end of March 2027
findings.quote: 2 High 2 Medium 1 Low

findings.headline: Council tax and NDR debtor and creditor review was not completed before the 2025/26 accounts and is now hoped for the 2026/27 closedown
findings.detail: The paper says extensive work with external consultants on council tax and NDR was not completed before the 2025/26 accounts were compiled. It hopes the review will be finished in time for the 2026/27 closedown, and EY had listed this area as a focus from prior years.
findings.matters: Council tax and NDR debtors and creditors are large balances for billing authorities, and a deferred review pushes the assurance on them into the following year's closedown.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: Unfortunately, this was not completed before complication of the accounts for 2025/26.

findings.headline: IFRS16 valuations received after the July 2026 Statement of Accounts used best estimates, with EY possibly unable to review the working papers before the December committee
findings.detail: The paper says a best estimate on valuations was used when the accounts were published in July 2026, and that the final valuations have now been received and working papers produced. It says these have been shared with EY, which may not be able to review them before the next Audit Committee.
findings.matters: Replacing estimated lease valuations with final figures under IFRS16 can change reported lease balances, so other councils that used estimates may face the same audit timing question.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: These valuations have now been received, the changes understood and working papers produced.

findings.headline: Work on capital grants and contributions has made significant progress, with conclusion expected shortly, the paper says
findings.detail: The paper says the council has provided extensive evidence to substantiate the capital grants and contributions figure. It hopes a final position will be agreed with EY before any further changes to the Statement of Accounts.
findings.matters: Capital grant and contribution balances are a recurring audit focus for councils, so a finance director would want to see whether the agreed figure is settled before the accounts are finalised.
findings.figures: None given in the paper.
findings.quote: It is expected that this will be concluded shortly as we’ve provided extensive evidence to substantiate the figure.

findings.headline: EY has highlighted three audit differences, two of them presentational misclassifications and the third on NNDR appeals still under discussion
findings.detail: The paper says the audit differences are on page 6 of the EY report and have not yet been applied to a revised Statement of Accounts. It says the two misclassifications are presentational only, and the NNDR appeals item is still being discussed with the auditor before any agreement is made.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit differences on business rates appeals can change the accounts before sign-off, so a finance director would want to know which items remain open.
findings.figures: Three audit differences; two misclassifications; the third item relates to NNDR appeals.
findings.quote: The 2 misclassifications are presentational only and do not affect our reported position or the fundamental reading of the accounts.

findings.headline: EY reports no major issues so far affecting the 31 January 2027 audit backstop deadline for the 2025/26 accounts
findings.detail: The paper says the audit cut-off date is 31 January 2027, and that no major concerns have been raised over timeliness of responses. It describes the overall progress position as good, with EY's next update due on 15 December 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, can use the backstop date and the current progress status to judge whether this council is on track to publish audited accounts on time.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 31 January 2027. Next EY update: 15 December 2026.
findings.quote: At present no major issues affecting the backstop deadline have been raised

findings.headline: Maturity profile runs from 2028/29 to 2042/43, with the £76.4 million maturity loans unchanged in the period
findings.detail: The paper reports that the earliest loan to mature is in 2028/29 and the latest in 2042/43. Within the table, the maturity-type loans stay at £76,400,000 with no repayments. The annuity loans are the ones being amortised.
findings.matters: A lender can see when the council's refinancing exposure begins and that the bulk of the debt is bullet maturity rather than amortising.
findings.figures: Earliest maturity 2028/29; latest maturity 2042/43; £76,400,000 maturity loans; £37,027,595 annuity closing value
findings.quote: The earliest loan to mature is in 2028/29 and the latest being 2042/43.

findings.headline: £114.077 million of external borrowing, all from PWLB, at rates of 1.95% to 2.76%, with no new loans taken in 2026/27 so far
findings.detail: The paper says the council's external borrowing at 30 September 2026 was £114.077 million, all held with the PWLB. It reports that the rates on these loans are 1.95% to 2.76%, against the c5.5+% it puts as currently available. It records that no new loans have been taken out so far this year, and that the annuity loans fell by £1,015,976 over the period.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director can see the size, lender concentration and coupon range of the debt book, and that no replacement borrowing has been needed so far.
findings.figures: £114.077 million external borrowing; 1.95% to 2.76% coupons; c5.5+% current rates; £1,015,976 annuity repayments; £1.347 million YTD interest costs
findings.quote: The Councils external borrowing at 30th September 2026 was £114.077 million, and these are all held with Public Works Loan Board (PWLB).

findings.headline: Deposit rates for 3+ months are above the 4% average assumed in the MTFS, on £70 million on deposit
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS target assumed £70 million on deposit during the year at an average of 4%. It states that the Bank of England base rate has been held at 3.75% over the first six months. It reports that current deposit rates for 3+ months are above the 4% estimate.
findings.matters: Another council's finance officer comparing budget assumptions with market deposit rates in the same period would find a specific, quantified example.
findings.figures: £70 million on deposit; 4% average assumed in the MTFS; 3.75% Bank of England base rate; deposits at 3.76% to 4.50% in the table
findings.quote: The current rates available to us for deposits for 3+ months are above this estimate.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to meet the £2.910 million budget for 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says the council is forecasting to achieve its investment income budget. It reports £0.529 million already received from matured investments, and estimates £1.379 million from the current deposits. The section 151 officer says the council is on track for the income expected from the budget-setting process.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see that a budgeted income line is on course, with the realised and forecast figures separated.
findings.figures: £2.910 million budget; £0.529 million received from matured investments; £1.379 million estimated income from current investments in 2026/27
findings.quote: From the Investment opportunities, the Council is forecasting to achieve its budget of £2.910 million.

findings.paper_title: 2. EHDC Audit Committee - Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Covering Report)
findings.headline: Overdue internal audit management actions fell to four from 18 reported in September 2026, with eight review areas closed
findings.detail: Management has confirmed that all actions are completed or closed for eight previous review areas. The paper reports the total of overdue actions has significantly reduced from the position reported to the Committee in September 2026.
findings.matters: A falling backlog of overdue control actions is a measurable sign of how quickly an authority is closing gaps that auditors have raised, which peers and lenders can compare across councils.
findings.figures: Overdue actions: four (18 in September 2026); eight previous review areas with all actions completed or closed
findings.quote: The total number of overdue actions (four) has significantly reduced from the position previously reported to the Committee in September 2026 (18 in total).

findings.paper_title: 2. EHDC Audit Committee - Internal Audit Progress Report October 2026 (Covering Report)
findings.headline: Procurement internal audit concluded with a ‘Limited’ assurance opinion, with most management actions now implemented
findings.detail: The paper reports that the Procurement audit has been finalised with a 'Limited' opinion and that management has taken prompt action. It says most audit actions have been implemented, with the final changes relating to updates to the computer system expected in place by the end of March 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would care about a Limited opinion on a high-spend control area and whether the remediation is on track to meet its stated deadline.
findings.figures: Procurement audit: 'Limited' assurance opinion; remaining computer-system changes expected by end of March 2027
findings.quote: The audit of Procurement has been finalised, which concluded with a ‘Limited’ assurance opinion

findings.headline: Council consciously elected to invest asset sale proceeds in deposits rather than reduce £115 million in PWLB debt.
findings.detail: The capital receipts from asset disposals were explicitly ringfenced for Treasury Management deposits instead of debt repayment. No new PWLB loans were taken in 2025/26, but the council's external borrowing remains £115.093 million, with only scheduled repayments of £2.008 million made.
findings.matters: This shows the council chose to maintain debt levels despite having proceeds available, reflecting deliberate capital strategy and priorities. The council is paying £2.718 million annually in borrowing costs while generating £1.666 million in deposit returns—a net negative carry position.
findings.figures: £115.093 million external borrowing; £2.718 million borrowing costs; £1.666 million deposit income; £45 million in new deposits
findings.quote: Per the roadmap, the capital receipts were ringfenced for investing in Treasury Management and not to repay the PWLB loans.

findings.headline: Council disposed of investment portfolio assets to replace income now lost, generating £1.666 million from temporary deposits instead.
findings.detail: The council sold investment and operational assets during 2025/26, deploying approximately £45 million in new deposits to generate treasury income. The paper explicitly states this new income stream is required because the council's existing Investment Portfolio income has reduced. This is a deliberate strategic shift following a property roadmap.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know the council has lost a revenue stream, forcing a shift to temporary deposits rather than permanent income sources. These deposits will mature between April and December 2026, creating a question about income continuity.
findings.figures: £45 million increase in deposits from 2024/25 to 2025/26; £1.666 million generated in 2025/26; deposits maturing at various dates through December 2026
findings.quote: The Treasury Management interest generated from the deposits is required to replace the reduced income from the Investment Portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A EHDC Quarterly Performance Report Q4
findings.headline: Rising homelessness with explicit warnings of sustained future increases due to Renters Rights Act implementation
findings.detail: Homelessness approaches have risen this quarter, particularly due to landlords serving notice before the Renters Rights Act takes effect. The council warns: 'Longer term this may result in a reduction of private rented units available within the district, which is likely to further increase homelessness approaches' and that supporting these cases will 'lead to more officer time and much longer cases, as court delay for defending possession proceedings are expected.' Households in temporary B&B accommodation rose from 17 at start of year to 30 by end of Q4.
findings.matters: Anticipated sustained increases in homelessness could create significant budget pressures, particularly for temporary accommodation costs and officer time if the council cannot contain demand.
findings.figures: Households in B&B: 30 at end Q4 (up from 17 at start of year); homelessness acceptances Q1-Q4: 0, 7, 13, 8
findings.quote: Longer term this may result in a reduction of private rented units available within the district, which is likely to further increase homelessness approaches. Supporting future homelessness approaches from private rented accommodation will also lead to more officer time and much longer cases, as court delay for defending possession proceedings are expected.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A EHDC Quarterly Performance Report Q4
findings.headline: Corporate Services budget overspend of £0.382m with no explanation provided in the report
findings.detail: Corporate Services had a budget of £5.764m with an outturn of £6.145m, resulting in a £0.382m (6.6%) overspend. This variance is not explained in the narrative sections. Corporate Services includes Legal, Democratic Services, Elections, HR, IT, and Communications. The unexplained nature of the overspend raises questions about budget control.
findings.matters: Material departmental overspends without explanation could indicate budget control weaknesses or hidden cost pressures that might recur.
findings.figures: Budget: £5.764 million, Outturn: £6.145 million, Variance: £0.382 million
findings.quote:
Budget: £5.764 million
Outturn: £6.145 million
Variance: £0.382 million

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio incurring £0.400m in legal and holding costs on a surplus asset
findings.detail: The council drew £0.400m from reserves for legal and holding costs on an investment property, suggesting the asset is not generating expected returns or is otherwise underutilised. No detail is given on the property, its acquisition cost, or recovery timeline.
findings.matters: Property holdings that generate costs rather than revenue indicate either poor asset management decisions or market conditions affecting expected returns, both of which are material for a lender assessing council financial resilience.
findings.figures: £0.400 million drawdown for investment property legal and holding costs
findings.quote: There was also a drawdown relating to the costs associated with our Investment Portfolio whereby we have incurred legal and holding costs (£0.400 million).

findings.headline: IT/Digital services face persistent cost pressures from Azure and licence escalation above inflation
findings.detail: IT/Digital overspent by £0.249m, primarily from Azure environment and licence costs increasing faster than inflation. The council expects ongoing pressure but states it has been factored into 2026/27 budgets; however, this signals structural cost growth in a key enabling function.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled IT cost escalation is a budget sustainability risk, particularly if inflation-beating increases continue.
findings.figures: £0.249 million overspend; contract increases above inflation
findings.quote: IT/Digital - £0.249 million, additional pressures to deliver our IT infrastructure, mainly our Azure environment and Licences. In addition, the annual increases on key contracts have been above inflation.

findings.headline: Waste contractor (EH Norse) requested additional £0.625m in-year
findings.detail: The council's waste services contractor submitted an unbudgeted cost escalation of £0.625m mid-year. The council absorbed this by drawing down a grant (Simpler Recycling Grant), masking the pressure in the headline outturn but creating a one-off funding dependency.
findings.matters: Contractor cost escalations above budget indicate either poor contract terms or market-driven cost pressures that may recur, especially given waste services are critical infrastructure.
findings.figures: £0.625 million additional request from EH Norse; offset by Simpler Recycling Grant drawdown
findings.quote: Waste Services – this is showing a balanced position however this is factoring in an additional request of £0.625 million from EH Norse which has been offset by a draw down from the Simpler Recycling Grant funding that EHDC received.

findings.headline: Wetside capital project delayed with £1.694m rolled forward to 2026/27
findings.detail: A major capital scheme has experienced unexpected delays, with £1.694m of the approved budget deferred. The report does not explain the nature of the delay, timing for completion, or whether this affects other planned schemes.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery is a key indicator of council management capability and resource planning for a lender. Unexplained delays with no clear recovery date are a red flag.
findings.figures: £1.694 million deferred; total capital budget £9.304 million (18% of programme)
findings.quote: Wetside (£1.694 million) related to unexpected delays in the project, funding has been rolled forward into 2026/27 Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Capital programme must make significant positive contribution to close the council's medium-term structural revenue budget deficit
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly requires that the capital programme must 'make a positive overall financial contribution to the Council's medium term revenue position' with 'a significant impact on the Council's revenue structural budget gap.' This shows the council is dependent on capital scheme yields, asset income, and disposals to help fund revenue operations and close a structural deficit.
findings.matters: Structural reliance on capital returns to offset revenue deficits creates performance risk: if capital investments underdeliver, property disposals fall short, or yields decline, the revenue gap widens. Lenders need to assess whether this sustainability model is robust.
findings.figures: Investment property portfolio £95,960k generating 7.14% gross yield (£6.585m rental income); capital receipts reserve £5.410m as at March 2025; example ratios given: £10m capital outlay at 1% net return yields £0.1m annual revenue
findings.quote: it will be necessary to ensure that the capital programme makes a positive overall financial contribution to the Council's medium term revenue position

findings.headline: PWLB maturity loans beginning to end from 2028/29 with higher refinancing costs already factored into MTFS
findings.detail: The council holds Public Work Loan Board (PWLB) borrowing split between annuity and maturity loans, with the earliest maturity loans due to end in 2028/29. The strategy explicitly notes that refinancing costs arising from higher interest rates have been factored into the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) for both 2028/29 and 2029/30, indicating this is a known and material cost pressure point.
findings.matters: A debt refinancing cliff starting in 2028/29 at elevated rates represents material refinancing risk. Lenders need to understand the council's capacity to service this known debt cost spike and whether revenue budgets can absorb it.
findings.figures: Maturity loans earliest end date 2028/29; refinancing costs factored into MTFS for 2028/29 and 2029/30
findings.quote: The Refinancing costs due to future interest higher rates have been factored into the MTFS in 2028/29 and 2029/30.

findings.headline: MRP policy change to lower annual contributions, with VRP decision deferred pending budget review—indicating financial uncertainty
findings.detail: Council moving to weighted-average MRP calculation, which will lower the annual MRP charge. However, to offset this reduction, the council plans to make Voluntary Revenue Provision (VRP) payments—but explicitly states it will 'review financial position before deciding whether to process a VRP payment for 2026/27.' This contingency approach signals budget tightness and the possibility of deferring the VRP.
findings.matters: A deferred VRP decision suggests the council may be facing General Fund pressure and wants to preserve budget flexibility; it also indicates the MRP saving is being factored in as available contingency rather than committed improvement
findings.figures: MRP forecast: 2024/25 £1,404k → 2026/27 £950k (reduction of £454k annually due to policy change)
findings.quote: Schedule 3 states: 'This change in approach will lower the MRP contribution required on an annual basis which in turn will impact the Council's Capital Financing Requirement. To lessen this, the Council will introduce Voluntary Revenue Provision (VRP)' and 'The Council will review is financial position before deciding whether to process a VRP payment for 2026/27'

findings.headline: Capital expenditure spiked to £14.7m in 2026/27, a 58% increase, with property acquisition flagged as possible reason
findings.detail: Capital spend forecast to jump from £9.3m to £14.7m in 2026/27, then drop sharply to £3.7m in subsequent years. The strategy notes the council 'may acquire property sites for strategic, operational and regeneration purposes', and that any such expenditure beyond existing capital receipts would require additional borrowing. No new borrowing is currently planned for the spike, suggesting it will be funded from existing resources or capital receipts, but this constrains future flexibility.
findings.matters: A capital spike of this size, especially if property-driven, can trigger rating concerns and debt covenant issues; the absence of planned borrowing means it's being funded from already-tightening reserves
findings.quote: Schedule 2 Section 2 shows capital expenditure of '9,304' for 2025/26 and '14,683' for 2026/27, with 'Borrowing Requirement -' across all years

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to fall by £2.86m annually, a structural loss of 42% in treasury returns
findings.detail: Investment income drops from £6,858k (2024/25 actual) to £4,000k from 2026/27 onwards. Although interest receivable rises from £1,530k to £2,912k, this only partially offsets the broader decline. This reduction directly impacts the General Fund balance and represents a material change in the council's budget resilience.
findings.matters: Treasury income is a source of flexibility in the budget; this sustained reduction means less cushion for service pressures or unexpected costs, forcing either spending cuts or higher council tax
findings.figures: Investment income: £6,858k (2024/25) → £4,000k (2026/27 onwards); Interest receivable: £1,530k → £2,912k
findings.quote: Schedule 2 Section 1 shows 'Investment Income (6,858)' for 2024/25 actuals and '(4,000)' for 2026/27 onwards

findings.headline: Cash reserves have fallen by £8.8m to £22.3m, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: Total investments dropped from £31.136m in 2024 to £22.287m by March 2025, with further anticipated decline to c£20m by end of 2025/26. This represents a 36% reduction in liquid resources over two years. The council is holding the minimum cash needed for short-term operational needs.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund contingencies without borrowing, directly affecting debt service resilience
findings.figures: Total investments: £31,136k (2024) → £22,287k (2025) → c£20,000k (2026 forecast)
findings.quote: Table 7.1 shows 'Value as at 31/03/2025' of £22,287k total investments (£7,287k NatWest and £15,000k External Investments), versus £31,136k the prior year

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Full ICT infrastructure review underway with indication that additional investment will be required
findings.detail: The council has commissioned a review of ICT infrastructure and staffing. 'This review is still being finalised, but the early indications is that there will be a requirement for additional investment in this area, to assist with the transition to the new Council structure.' The current budget provision is £497k but 'subject to full business cases before the money is released.'
findings.matters: Unquantified future IT investment needs create budget uncertainty; if the review reveals larger requirements than budgeted, additional capital or revenue will be needed during a period of governance transition.
findings.figures: £497k budgeted; final requirement to be determined by business case
findings.quote: This review is still being finalised, but the early indications is that there will be a requirement for additional investment in this area, to assist with the transition to the new Council structure.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Loss of Hampshire Business Rates pool income in 2026/27 removes expected additional funding
findings.detail: The council received additional income from a Hampshire business rates pool in 2025/26. 'This pool will not continue in 2026/27 due to the expected future changes of local government structure in Hampshire.' This reduces revenue availability.
findings.matters: Loss of pooled income is a real reduction in available resources; the document does not quantify the impact, but it is a material change from prior year.
findings.figures: Pool income amount not disclosed; pool ending in 2026/27
findings.quote: This pool will not continue in 2026/27 due to the expected future changes of local government structure in Hampshire.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio generating essential income but under economic pressure and recently restructured
findings.detail: The council's investment property portfolio helps keep council tax lower and is a material income source. However, the council notes it is 'open to the pressures of the current economic climate' and states: 'After extensive work, the Council has made changes to the portfolio to help mitigate risks in this area.' Income varies year to year with vacancies and relets.
findings.matters: A council depending on investment property returns is exposed to real estate market downturns; recent restructuring suggests prior performance issues or risk management concerns that warrant monitoring.
findings.figures: Investment property income undisclosed; referenced as material to keeping council tax lower
findings.quote: After extensive work, the Council has made changes to the portfolio to help mitigate risks in this area.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Waste contract final figures not agreed; council budgeting £447k growth on assumption
findings.detail: The council has allocated £447k for waste inflationary growth and is introducing food waste collections in 2026/27, but the final business plan with their contractor (Norse) has not been agreed. The document states: 'The final business plan agreement has not been agreed for 2026/27 yet with Norse, but this will be agreed before the start of the new financial year.'
findings.matters: Major contracted services (waste is a significant budget item) without finalized costs create budget risk; if actual costs exceed the £447k allocation, it could force mid-year adjustments or further draw on reserves.
findings.figures: £447 million waste inflationary growth budgeted; food waste introduction costs being finalized
findings.quote: The final business plan agreement has not been agreed for 2026/27 yet with Norse, but this will be agreed before the start of the new financial year.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation uncertainty is forcing council to rebuild savings plan mid-cycle
findings.detail: The government announced plans to abolish district councils and create unitary authorities. The council has refocussed its transformation programme as a result: 'Since the announcement of the governance changes to local government in Hampshire, the whole project was reviewed and refocussed. Some of the proposed changes and savings were not deliverable within the remaining period of the Council.' The decision on governance is expected in Spring 2026.
findings.matters: Structural uncertainty is forcing the council to abandon planned savings mid-cycle and adjust strategy, making forecasts less reliable. A lender needs to know whether the council will exist in its current form to repay debt.
findings.figures: Decision expected Spring 2026; some planned savings abandoned
findings.quote: Since the announcement of the governance changes to local government in Hampshire, the whole project was reviewed and refocussed. Some of the proposed changes and savings were not deliverable within the remaining period of the Council.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Growing savings gap of £640k in 2027/28 and £1.020m in 2028/29 with no detailed plan
findings.detail: The council acknowledges future funding shortfalls but relies on transformation programmes to deliver savings. The MTFS shows required savings of £640k for 2027/28 and £1.020m for 2028/29. The council states it is 'confident that the savings can be achieved in the future' but offers only general reassurance rather than specific plans.
findings.matters: Unspecified savings gaps in the near term are a material risk; councils that cannot articulate how they will balance budgets are riskier borrowers, particularly when relying on transformation that is already being disrupted by government changes.
findings.figures: £0.640 million for 2027/28 and £1.020 million for 2028/29
findings.quote: The figure for future years are £0.640 million for 2027/28 and £1.020 million for 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: EHDC Full Council Budget Report 2627 v2
findings.headline: Large drawdown from earmarked reserves of £2.146 million is explicitly not sustainable
findings.detail: The council is drawing £2.146m from earmarked reserves in 2026/27 to fund specific projects and commitments. The CFO explicitly states this is not sustainable: 'However, it must be noted that this is a large draw form reserves, and so not sustainable at these levels for future years.' The reserve balance is forecast to fall from £10.103m to £8.007m.
findings.matters: Large, unsustainable reserve drawdowns suggest the council is using one-off money to balance the day-to-day budget, which weakens medium-term financial resilience and is a red flag for lenders.
findings.figures: £2.146 million drawdown; reserves fall from £10.103m to £8.007m
findings.quote: However, it must be noted that this is a large draw form reserves, and so not sustainable at these levels for future years.

findings.headline: Pension scheme actuary error identified in fair value of plan assets valuation
findings.detail: Management received an updated IAS 19 pension report from the actuary that identified an error in the calculation of the net pension liability, specifically a £1.3m difference in the fair value of plan assets. While the auditor notes this did not impact the net pension figure due to asset ceiling restrictions, it indicates quality control lapses in the actuarial work and pension accounting.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically a council's largest balance sheet liability; errors in actuarial valuations could mask material misstatements in the financial position.
findings.figures: c.£1.3m difference in fair value of plan assets disclosure
findings.quote: Management have received an updated IAS 19 report which shows a c.£1.3m difference in the fair value of plan assets but this had no impact on the net pension figure, only impacting the pensions disclosures.

findings.headline: Council failed to implement IFRS 16 leasing standard as required, blocking audit progress
findings.detail: IFRS 16 became mandatory on 1 April 2024, and the council was required to prepare accounts under this standard. However, the initial draft accounts were prepared under the old IAS 17 standard instead. This compliance failure is preventing audit work from progressing and indicates a significant gap in accounting infrastructure or competence.
findings.matters: Failure to implement mandatory accounting standards on time signals governance and technical capability issues that could lead to further compliance problems.
findings.figures: None provided - policy/timeline breach
findings.quote: Management were required by the CIPFA Code of Accounting Practice to prepare the draft accounts for the requirements of IFRS 16 which is effective from 1 April 2024. However, leasing arrangements in the initial draft statement of accounts were prepared under the old accounting standard IAS 17. Therefore, at the present time we cannot progress this area.

findings.headline: Prior period adjustment of £11.6m required for capital grants received in advance due to historical understatement
findings.detail: Management has identified a probable understatement of approximately £11.6m in the opening balance for capital grants received in advance. This significant adjustment will require prior period restatement in the 2024/25 financial statements, indicating weaknesses in prior-year recording and reconciliation controls over capital grants.
findings.matters: A material prior period adjustment suggests control weaknesses over capital funding tracking and risks future misstatement of capital resources and funding profiles.
findings.figures: c.£11.6m understatement of opening balance for Capital Grants received in advance
findings.quote: This has identified a probable understatement of c.£11.6m in the opening balance for Capital Grants received in advance and, subject to our testing, would require a prior period adjustment.

findings.headline: Council tax and NDR debtor/creditor reconciliation unresolved for second consecutive year, with unreconciled variance growing
findings.detail: The council failed to reconcile council tax and business rates accounting models to the financial statements in 2023/24, resulting in a qualified audit opinion. Progress has been made in 2024/25 but a material unreconciled difference of £4.8m remains in opening balances, and this difference has grown by another £3m in the current year. The auditor warns that failure to resolve this risks another limitation of scope and qualified opinion.
findings.matters: A second consecutive qualified audit opinion would damage creditor confidence and suggests weak financial controls over major revenue streams and receivables management.
findings.figures: £4.8m unreconciled difference in opening balances; additional £3m growth in current year; material balances unable to be supported
findings.quote: Management have made some progress in reconciling the financial statements to the council tax and business rate accounting models but there remains an unreconciled difference of £4.8m within the opening balances which management are still trying to resolve. This unreconciled difference has increased in the current year by another c.£3m. If these balances are not reconciled there is a risk that the Council will not be able to support these balances in the 2024/25 financial statements and will lead to another limitation of scope.
